title: Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi inaugurates and lays foundation stone of Pune Metro projects worth around ₹21,800 Crore
subtitle:
A better-connected Pune is a faster-growing Pune; New Metro projects will boost the city's growth and improve Ease of Living: PM

Pune is a hub of dreams and aspirations for the nation's youth, the strengthening metro connectivity is set to provide a new impetus to the development of Pune city: PM

Our cities are not merely residential spaces, they are major centers of the nation's economic activity, we must develop hundreds of small cities across the country into active growth hubs: PM

Today, India stands as a nation that is not only the fastest-growing economy, but also the fastest poverty reducer: PM
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 2:43PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi inaugurated and laid the foundation stone for Pune Metro projects worth around ₹21,800 crore today through video conferencing. Addressing the gathering on the occasion, the Prime Minister extended warm Diwali greetings to the people of Pune and Maharashtra and remarked that festive joy multiplies when new public conveniences are added to daily life. Recalling how he laid the foundation stone for the first phase of the Pune Metro ten years ago, he noted that the inauguration of the Hinjawadi to Shivajinagar corridor will provide superior connectivity to a major IT hub while the new line initiated today will further link the old and new parts of the city.
Describing Pune as a historic center of ideas that has consistently guided the nation and society, the Prime Minister stated that the city is now channeling the fresh energy of a Viksit Bharat across IT, automobiles, pharmaceuticals, startups, innovation, and manufacturing as a hub of youth aspirations. “And in such a scenario, the strengthening metro connectivity here is going to give new momentum to the development of Pune city,” noted PM Modi.
Explaining that the expansion of the Pune Metro reflects how modern cities are being shaped for a Viksit Bharat, the Prime Minister observed that beyond traditional markers like industries, cuisine, or local produce, urban centers are now judged by their competitiveness and Ease of Living, both of which are enhanced by metro networks that save commuting time and offer greater convenience. He pointed out that saving a city's time boosts urban productivity, which in turn accelerates the national economy. “And when the economy grows, both the poor and the middle class benefit from it,” asserted Shri Modi.
Citing the occasion as a prime example of pro-people and proactive governance, the Prime Minister highlighted that over the past 12 years, India's metro network has expanded to nearly 1,200 kilometers across 26 cities serving over one crore daily commuters. “Today the Indian metro network is counted among the top three metro networks in the world,” noted PM Modi.
Observing that Maharashtra mirrored the national transformation since 2014 when only 10 to 11 kilometers of metro lines were operational in the state, the Prime Minister pointed out that nearly 175 kilometers are now in service while construction is underway on over 680 kilometers with an investment exceeding 2.5 lakh crore rupees. “This money is going into the pockets of laborers, this money is giving employment to engineers, and this money is creating employment in shops and in factories,” observed Shri Modi.
Highlighting another distinctive aspect of the newly inaugurated corridor, the Prime Minister noted that the metro line has been constructed under the Public-Private Partnership model through the combined efforts of the government and the private sector. “This is such a model of development whose success gives further momentum to the progress of the country,” remarked PM Modi.
Stating that every citizen and young son and daughter of India is working to build a Viksit Bharat with the nationwide spirit of 'We Will Do It', the Prime Minister noted that over the past 12 years the nation focused its energy on building rural roads, highways, expressways, new and electrified rail lines, long tunnels, and high bridges. “Now in the coming years along with this, the country is going to invest its energy in making its cities among the best cities in the world,” asserted Shri Modi.
Emphasizing that cities are major engines of economic activity rather than mere residential spaces and that hundreds of smaller towns must be transformed into growth hubs, the Prime Minister highlighted the approval of the Urban Challenge Fund in February this year backed by one lakh crore rupees in Central assistance to mobilize lakhs of crores in urban investment. He urged local bodies and private sector partners to join this effort in mission mode. “I am confident that Maharashtra will expand its role in this even further,” affirmed PM Modi.
Pointing out two major achievements driving global discussion about India, the Prime Minister noted that the nation has maintained the world's fastest growth rate amid difficult international conditions while lifting 50 crore citizens out of extreme poverty within just 10 to 12 years according to the latest World Bank report, moving beyond decades of mere slogans for generations. “Earlier, the fight against poverty was only in slogans, today India is defeating poverty on the ground,” asserted Shri Modi.
Observing that India's twin milestones as the fastest-growing economy and the fastest poverty reducer are interlinked, the Prime Minister explained that a growing economy and expanding budget enable higher public investment, while money once lost to scams and leakages now reaches beneficiaries directly. He added that treasury investments in roads, rail, airports, metros, electricity, water, and gas pipelines simultaneously improve living standards and generate employment. “Both these accomplishments are connected to each other,” noted PM Modi.
Highlighting the impact of welfare deliveries such as houses for the poor, toilets, Har Ghar Jal tap water connections, and cooking gas connections, the Prime Minister stated that these essential amenities have boosted public self-confidence and saved valuable daily time. “And this time is being utilized in earning extra income for their families,” observed Shri Modi.
Recalling his completion of 25 years as head of a government last month guided by the mantra that empowering the poor gives them the courage to overcome poverty, the Prime Minister reflected on initiating Garib Kalyan Melas as Chief Minister of Gujarat to focus on scheme delivery and invite beneficiaries onto the stage to take a pledge against poverty. “They used to take a resolution to defeat poverty and return from the event carrying self-confidence,” remarked PM Modi.
Stating that the mission initiated back then has continued uninterrupted as true good governance defined by the 'Power to Empower', the Prime Minister emphasized that this transformation is the result of years of deliberate and planned efforts rather than a sudden occurrence. “Therefore, 50 crore Indians have defeated poverty,” noted Shri Modi.
Explaining that poverty reduction benefits the wider nation beyond the families escaping deprivation, the Prime Minister pointed out that it revitalizes the national economy and creates a new middle class whose purchasing power drives market demand and opens new possibilities from shops to factories. “Meaning, decreasing poverty in India is taking the economy of India to a new height,” observed PM Modi.
Underscoring the vital role of farmers in the Viksit Bharat journey and the government's continuous efforts to empower them, the Prime Minister acknowledged the severe hardships currently faced by farming families in Maharashtra due to adverse weather and natural calamity despite extensive water conservation work under Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis in recent years. Expressing full sensitivity and solidarity on behalf of the government while noting his awareness of the drought, the provision of advance assistance by the state government, and the transfer of PM Kisan funds, he reassured the state's cultivators. “Do not worry at all, we are all with the farmers,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Reminding citizens during this festive season of their social responsibility to remember drought-affected citizens, farming families, and others in distress so that the joy of Diwali remains in their homes as well, the Prime Minister urged the nation to stand united in overcoming the calamity. “Only together will we face this calamity,” asserted PM Modi.
Concluding his address with best wishes for the metro projects, the Prime Minister emphasized that collective and united effort, Sabka Prayas, serves as the lifeblood of a Viksit Bharat. “With this very spirit, we have to remain engaged in the development of the country,” affirmed Shri Modi.

title: English rendering of PM’s address at the Foundation Stone Laying Ceremony of Pune Metro Projects via video conferencing
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 2:29PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Governor of Maharashtra Shri Jishnu Dev Varma ji, Chief Minister Shri Devendra Fadnavis ji, my colleague in the Union Cabinet Shri Manohar Lal ji, Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Shri Eknath Shinde ji, Smt. Sunetra Ajit Pawar ji, all ministers, Members of Parliament and Members of the Legislative Assembly, other public representatives, and my dear brothers and sisters of Pune!
Diwali is just around the corner. First of all, I extend my heartfelt greetings to all of you on the occasion of Diwali!
Friends,
The joy of festivals becomes even greater when a new facility is added to people's lives. Today is such a happy occasion for the people of Pune. I am pleased that another line of the Pune Metro is being inaugurated today. Ten years ago, I had the opportunity to lay the foundation stone for the first phase of this project in Pune. With the metro now starting between Hinjawadi and Shivajinagar, one of Pune’s major IT hubs will receive improved connectivity. The new line whose work has commenced today will further strengthen connectivity between the old and new parts of Pune. I extend my heartfelt congratulations to all the people of Pune and Maharashtra.
Friends,
Pune has always been a centre of ideas that have given new direction to the nation and to society. Today, Pune is also providing direction to the new energy of a Viksit Bharat. From IT, automobiles, pharmaceuticals, startups, innovation, and manufacturing, Pune is a place of dreams and aspirations for the youth of the country. In such a situation, the strengthening metro connectivity here is set to give a new momentum to the development of Pune city.
Friends,
The inauguration and expansion of the Pune Metro demonstrates how we are building cities for a Viksit Bharat. Earlier, a city's identity was defined by its industries, or by its famous cuisine, fruits, or crops. But today, two more benchmarks have been added to the identity of cities. First, how competitive a city is. Second, the level of ease of living it offers. Metro projects help improve both these parameters for any city. As Pune Metro expands, it is saving time and providing greater convenience to the residents of Pune. And we all know that when a city's time is saved, its productivity increases. When a city's productivity increases, the country's economy gains momentum. And when the economy grows, both the poor and the middle class benefit.
Friends,
Today is also an example of pro-people, proactive good governance. The first metro in our country began operating in 1984. In the thirty years that followed, only 248 kilometres of metro lines were built. Two hundred and forty-eight kilometres. Until 2014, metro services existed in only five cities of the country. Had the same old thinking continued, had the old government remained in place, had the old work culture continued, it would have taken many more decades for the metro to reach Pune. But when the people gave the NDA an opportunity to serve in 2014, we moved forward with a resolve. That resolve was to improve ease of living and ease of transportation for the middle class living in our cities. Today, we can see the results. Over the past twelve years, metro transportation in the country has undergone a complete transformation. From 248 kilometres of metro routes in 2014, the network has now expanded to nearly 1,200 kilometres. From only five cities having metro services in 2014, metro systems are now operating in 26 cities. More than one crore people are now travelling by metro every day. Today, India's metro network is counted among the top three metro networks in the world.
Friends,
The situation in Maharashtra was similar to that in the rest of the country. When the NDA's double-engine government was formed for the first time in 2014, Maharashtra had only around 10–11 kilometres of operational metro lines. Today, nearly 175 kilometres of metro lines are in service in Maharashtra. Work is underway on more than 680 kilometres of metro corridors. Today, investments of more than ₹2.5 lakh crore are being made in Maharashtra's metro infrastructure alone. This money is going into the pockets of workers. This money is generating employment for engineers. This money is creating jobs in shops and factories.
Friends,
This metro project is special for another reason as well. This metro line has been constructed on a PPP model. That is, it has been built through the joint efforts of the government and the private sector. This is a development model whose success will further accelerate the country's progress.
Friends,
Today, every citizen of India, every young son and daughter of India, is working with full strength to build a Viksit Bharat. Today everyone is confidently saying: We Will Do It. We Will Do It. This spirit exists throughout the country. Over the past twelve years, the nation’s energy has been reflected in village roads, highways, expressways, electrification of new railway lines, long tunnels, and towering bridges. Numerous projects and schemes are taking shape across the country. In the coming years, along with this, the country will devote its energy to making its cities among the best in the world.
Friends,
Our cities are not merely places to live. They are also major centres of economic activity. We must transform hundreds of small cities across the country into growth hubs. It was with this vision that the Urban Challenge Fund was approved in February this year. The central government is providing support of ₹1 lakh crore for this fund. The goal is to attract investments worth many lakh crores of rupees into cities across the country in the coming years. I urge local bodies, our friends in the private sector, and everyone else to come forward. We must all work in mission mode. I am confident that Maharashtra will expand its role further in this effort.
Friends,
There are two additional reasons why India is being discussed throughout the world today. First, India has maintained the fastest growth rate in the world despite difficult global circumstances. Second, within just ten to twelve years, fifty crore people in India have overcome extreme poverty. This fact has emerged in the latest World Bank report. Many generations in the country grew up hearing promises and claims about eradicating poverty. Earlier, the fight against poverty existed only in slogans. Today, India is defeating poverty on the ground.
Friends,
Today, India is the country that is both the fastest-growing economy and the fastest reducer of poverty. These two achievements are interconnected. India's economy is growing rapidly. India's budget is expanding. Investments in the people are increasing. The money that earlier disappeared through scams, favoritism, and leakages is now reaching beneficiaries directly. When the nation’s resources are invested in roads, railways, airports, and metro systems, when the government increases investment in electricity, water, and gas pipelines, people's lives improve and employment opportunities increase.
Friends,
Facilities such as homes for the poor, toilets, tap water for every household, and gas connections have increased people’s confidence and saved their time. And this saved time is being used to earn additional income for their families.
Friends,
Just last month, with your blessings, I completed twenty-five years as the head of government. The motto of our government has always been that when you empower the poor, the poor gain the courage to lift themselves out of poverty. I remember that when I was Chief Minister of Gujarat, I started the tradition of Garib Kalyan Melas with this very thought. These events focused on delivering welfare schemes directly to the poor. Poor citizens were invited onto the stage. They would take a pledge to defeat poverty and return home with renewed confidence.
Friends,
The work that I began twenty-five years ago continues uninterrupted even today. This is what I call Power to Empower. Power to Empower is true good governance. This transformation did not happen overnight. Previous governments grew tired of merely raising slogans. We connected every link. We wove together the dreams of millions of lives. This is the result of years of thoughtful and well-planned efforts. And that is why fifty crore Indians have defeated poverty.
Friends,
When poverty declines, the benefits are not limited to those families that escape it. It injects new energy into the country’s economy. It creates a new middle class. This neo-middle class brings new dreams. Its purchasing power drives markets. New opportunities emerge, from shops to factories. In other words, the reduction of poverty in India is taking the Indian economy to new heights.
Friends,
In this journey towards a Viksit Bharat, our farmer brothers and sisters also have a major role. Therefore, our government is continuously empowering farmers. However, due to adverse weather conditions in Maharashtra, many farming families are facing difficulties at present. Over the past few years, a great deal of work on water conservation has been done under the leadership of Devendra Fadnavis ji. But this natural disaster has created major challenges. I want to assure every farmer brother and sister in Maharashtra that in this difficult time, the NDA government stands firmly with them with full sensitivity and commitment. I am aware of the drought conditions in Maharashtra. The state government has already provided advance assistance as well. I have transferred the PM-Kisan funds. Please do not worry at all. We are standing with every farmer.
Friends,
I would also like to tell the people of the country that this is the season of festivals and celebrations. We must remember our farmer brothers and sisters. We must ensure that the joy of Diwali remains alive in their homes as well. This is also our social responsibility. We must not forget the difficulties faced by our drought-affected citizens, our farmers, and others living in villages. Together, we will face this challenge.
Friends,
Collective effort, united effort, is the lifebreath of a Viksit Bharat. With this spirit, we must remain dedicated to the development of the nation. Once again, my best wishes to all of you for these metro projects. My heartfelt greetings for the upcoming festivals. Thank you very much. People of Pune, repeat after me with full strength, raising both your hands:
Bharat Mata Ki Jai!
Bharat Mata Ki Jai!
Bharat Mata Ki Jai!

title: EVERY RUPEE OF PUBLIC MONEY MUST BE ACCOUNTED FOR AND UTILISED FOR ITS INTENDED PURPOSE: LOK SABHA SPEAKER
subtitle:
TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY ARE CORNERSTONES OF DEMOCRACY; PACs MUST ENSURE THAT PUBLIC EXPENDITURE TRANSLATES INTO TANGIBLE OUTCOMES FOR CITIZENS: LOK SABHA SPEAKER

LOK SABHA SPEAKER CALLS FOR TIME-BOUND RESOLUTION OF LONG-PENDING AUDIT OBSERVATIONS; POLITICAL DIFFERENCES MUST GIVE WAY TO A SHARED COMMITMENT TO FINANCIAL PROBITY AND NATIONAL WELFARE

LOK SABHA SPEAKER URGES PACs TO LEVERAGE AI, DATA ANALYTICS AND RESPONSIBLE TECHNOLOGY TO STRENGTHEN FINANCIAL OVERSIGHT AND PREVENT MISUSE OF PUBLIC FUNDS

LOK SABHA SPEAKER INAUGURATES CONFERENCE OF CHAIRPERSONS OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEES OF PARLIAMENT AND STATE/UT LEGISLATURES IN THIRUVANANTHAPURAM
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 3:51PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Lok Sabha Speaker Shri Om Birla today called upon the Public Accounts Committees (PACs) of Parliament and State Legislatures to strengthen their role as guardians of public money, emphasising that every rupee drawn from the public exchequer must be properly accounted for and utilised fully for the purpose for which it was sanctioned. He said that transparency and accountability are the cornerstones of democracy and that the ultimate measure of public expenditure must be the positive difference it makes to the lives of ordinary citizens.
Inaugurating the Conference of Chairpersons of Public Accounts Committees of Parliament and State Legislatures in Thiruvananthapuram, Shri Birla said that the PAC is a vital institution of parliamentary democracy, entrusted with the responsibility of examining public expenditure, ensuring financial discipline and holding the Executive accountable. He observed that the responsibility of the Committees extends beyond scrutiny of accounts and audit findings; they must also assess whether public funds have achieved their intended objectives and delivered the outcomes for which they were allocated.
Expressing concern over audit observations remaining unresolved for 10, 15 or even 20 years, Shri Birla said that such prolonged pendency raises serious questions about the effectiveness of the system. He called for a concrete, systematic and time-bound action plan to ensure that audit observations and the action arising from them are addressed without undue delay. The Union and State Governments, he said, must work together to strengthen the mechanisms of monitoring, review and follow-up so that accountability is not merely established on paper but translated into timely corrective action. Highlighting the distinctive democratic convention of appointing a Member of the Opposition as the Chairperson of the Public Accounts Committee, Shri Birla said that this practice reflects the maturity, inclusiveness and strength of India's parliamentary democracy. The representation of all political parties in the Committee ensures that different perspectives are brought to the examination of public expenditure. He described this arrangement as a shining example of the ability of democratic institutions to rise above political considerations in pursuit of a common national objective.
Lok Sabha Speaker noted that Members may belong to different political parties, hold different ideologies and have differing views on policies and governance; however, when it comes to safeguarding public money, their responsibility is shared. The PAC must function through dialogue, cooperation, consensus and collective responsibility. Its purpose is not to criticise any individual or government, but to ensure that public funds are neither misused nor wasted, that irregularities and leakages are prevented, and that the Executive remains accountable to the people. He emphasised that the trust of citizens is the foundation of democratic governance. Every rupee of public money represents the aspirations and contribution of the people and must therefore be spent with the highest standards of financial propriety.
Lok Sabha Speaker stressed that the assessment of public expenditure must not remain confined to figures, allocations and utilisation certificates. In the case of infrastructure projects, Committees should, wherever appropriate, visit project sites and examine the quality of work, its timely completion and adherence to prescribed standards. He said that such direct assessment would help establish whether the money spent has resulted in the intended infrastructure and whether public resources have been used effectively. Similarly, in the case of social welfare schemes, it is essential to go beyond the amount spent and examine the actual impact of the expenditure. The ultimate objective of public expenditure, he said, must be social good and public welfare.
Referring to the important role of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, Shri Birla said that the examination of CAG audit findings, scrutiny of Action Taken Reports and follow-up on recommendations are integral to the functioning of the PAC. However, the larger purpose of this exercise is to ensure that public money is used transparently, efficiently and strictly in accordance with its sanctioned purpose. Where systemic improvements are required, the Committees should provide appropriate guidance and recommend corrective measures. He called upon the PACs of Parliament and State Legislatures to use the conference as an effective platform for sharing experiences, ideas, innovations and best practices. He said that the practices adopted by States that have demonstrated greater transparency, stronger financial oversight and more effective evaluation should be shared so that others can learn from them. He underlined that healthy competition among States in strengthening accountability mechanisms would contribute to better governance across the country.
Stressing the need for a future-oriented approach, the Speaker said that changing circumstances require the Committees to continuously strengthen their methods of scrutiny and oversight. Technology, data analytics and Artificial Intelligence can play an important role in analysing large volumes of expenditure data, identifying emerging trends, detecting potential financial irregularities and improving the monitoring of audit observations. He also stressed the importance of citizen participation in governance and said that greater transparency in the use of public resources strengthens public confidence in democratic institutions. A system in which public expenditure is closely monitored, accounts are thoroughly scrutinised and corrective action is taken in a timely manner is essential for ensuring that government resources serve the people effectively. He observed that the scope and responsibilities of the PAC have evolved over the years. Apart from examining audit reports and public accounts, the Committee has made significant contributions through its recommendations on public expenditure, the functioning of government departments, administrative reforms and programme evaluation.
Recalling the recent centenary celebrations of the PAC, he said that the foundational principles of the Committee must continue to guide its future priorities and that the commitments made on that occasion should be translated into concrete improvements in its functioning. The Speaker further emphasised that schemes implemented through Centre-State partnerships and public-private partnerships require effective financial scrutiny within the respective mandates of the Committees.
Shri Birla expressed confidence that the deliberations would lead to constructive recommendations and concrete outcomes to strengthen financial discipline, transparency and accountability. He said that the resolutions emerging from the conference should guide improvements in monitoring, audit follow-up and the quality of public expenditure, with the shared objective of ensuring that every rupee of public money is utilised responsibly and for its intended purpose.
The Inaugural Session was graced and addressed by the Chief Minister of Keralam Shri V. D. Satheesan,; Deputy Chairman, Rajya Sabha, Shri  Harivansh; Chairman, Public Accounts Committee, Lok Sabha, Shri K. C. Venugopal; Speaker, Keralam Legislative Assembly, Shri Thiruvanchoor Radhakrishnan, and Chairperson, PAC of Keralam Legislative Assembly, Shri K. N. Balagopal. The Session was attended by Chairpersons and Members of Public Accounts Committees of State Legislatures, and  other distinguished dignitaries.
On this occasion, Public Accounts Committee Conference Souvenir 2026 was also released.
FINANCIAL SCRUTINY MUST BE OUTCOME-DRIVEN TO ENSURE ACCOUNTABILITY, SAYS CHAIRPERSON OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE OF PARLIAMENT OF INDIA; CALLS FOR TIMELY AUDITS AND BALANCED COVERAGE OF PUBLIC WELFARE PROGRAMMES
Delivering Welcome Address, Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Parliament of India, Shri K.C. Venugopal, underscored the need to strengthen legislative financial scrutiny to ensure that public expenditure translates into tangible outcomes, improved service delivery and meaningful benefits for citizens. Emphasising that accountability must go beyond the mere examination of expenditure, he called for a more outcome-oriented approach to parliamentary oversight, ensuring that every public rupee is spent judiciously and delivers its intended purpose. He also proposed that at least one PAC Report, along with the Government’s Action Taken thereon, be discussed during every Session of Parliament. He also underscored the importance of timely audits, balanced coverage of various sectors and closer scrutiny of flagship welfare programmes and major infrastructure projects to ensure that public resources serve the larger public interest.

मुझे ख़ुशी है कि सांस्कृतिक और प्राकृतिक रूप से मनोहारी प्रदेश केरलम की इस धरती पर, जहां लोकतांत्रिक परंपराएं समृद्ध रही हैं; संसद और राज्य विधानमंडलों की PAC के प्रतिनिधि एक साथ बैठकर “Audit, Accountability and Good Governance - The Evolving Role of the PAC” विषय पर विचार-विमर्श कर रहे हैं।

भारतीय लोकतांत्रिक व्यवस्था में Public Accounts Committee (लोक लेखा समिति) का एक ऐतिहासिक महत्व रहा है। आजादी से पहले भी इस समिति का अस्तित्व था और स्वतंत्रता के बाद भी हमने एक महत्वपूर्ण संसदीय परंपरा विकसित की, जिसके अंतर्गत विपक्ष के वरिष्ठ सदस्य को इस समिति का सभापति बनाया जाता है। इसका उद्देश्य यह सुनिश्चित करना है कि सार्वजनिक धन के उपयोग की निष्पक्ष और प्रभावी निगरानी हो। यह हमारे लोकतंत्र की एक बड़ी ताकत है, जिसमें सभी राजनीतिक दलों के प्रतिनिधि मिलकर कार्य करते हैं।

संसद और राज्य विधान मंडल कानून बनाते हैं तथा बजट पारित करते हैं। बजट के माध्यम से यह सुनिश्चित किया जाता है कि जनता का धन Infrastructure Development, Social Welfare Schemes और जनकल्याण के विभिन्न कार्यों पर खर्च हो। इस धन का निर्धारित उद्देश्यों के अनुरूप उपयोग सुनिश्चित करने में Public Accounts Committee की महत्वपूर्ण भूमिका होती है।
मेरा मानना है कि सामाजिक कल्याण की योजनाओं में केवल बजट आवंटन और धनराशि खर्च होना ही पर्याप्त नहीं है, बल्कि उस धन के उपयोग के बाद समाज पर उसका क्या प्रभाव पड़ा, इसका मूल्यांकन करना भी Public Accounts Committee की जिम्मेदारी है।
इस दिशा में यह समिति दल से ऊपर उठकर संसदीय निष्पक्षता के साथ काम करती है। क्योंकि Public Accounts Committee के कार्य में सभी का साझा उद्देश्य एक ही होता है - शासन में जवाबदेही सुनिश्चित करना और कार्यपालिका में पारदर्शिता लाना।

देश के विभिन्न प्रदेशों से इस सम्मेलन में शामिल हुए PAC के सभापतियों और सदस्यों का आह्वान किया कि बदलते परिप्रेक्ष्य में PAC के कामकाज को प्रभावी बनाने के लिए हमें बेहतर Technology का उपयोग करना होगा। Data Analysis और Artificial Intelligence के माध्यम से हम आंकड़ों का बेहतर विश्लेषण कर सकते हैं, खर्च के रुझानों को समझ सकते हैं, संभावित जोखिमों की पहचान कर सकते हैं और वित्तीय अनियमितताओं पर प्रभावी ढंग से अंकुश लगा सकते हैं। हालांकि Technology के साथ जवाबदेही और मानवीय संवेदनशीलता का भी समन्वय आवश्यक है, ताकि सरकारी धन का उपयोग केवल योजनाओं तक सीमित न रहे, बल्कि समाज के कल्याण और आम नागरिकों के जीवन में सकारात्मक परिवर्तन लाने में भी सहायक हो।

मुझे आशा है कि दो दिनों के इस सम्मेलन में संसद तथा राज्य विधानमंडलों की Public Accounts Committees अपने अनुभवों, विचारों और दृष्टिकोणों को साझा करेंगी, एक-दूसरे की best practices से सीखेंगी, उपयोगी सुझाव सामने आएंगे; जिससे हम अपनी लोक लेखा समितियों को और अधिक मजबूत तथा प्रभावी बनाने की दिशा में आगे बढ़ेंगे।

title: SUVIKALP- Mine Repurposing Tool; Transforming Closed and Abandoned Mines into Productive Assets
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 1:30PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Mine closure is an integral part of the mining lifecycle. However, the responsibility towards a mining region does not end with the completion of mining operations. Ensuring productive utilisation of post-mining land, environmental restoration and sustainable socio-economic development requires a structured approach to mine repurposing. Recognising this need, the Coal Controller Organisation (CCO), under the Ministry of Coal, Government of India, has developed
SUVIKALP – Mine Repurposing Tool
, a digital decision-support platform aligned with the
Mining Plan Guidelines for Coal and Lignite Mine, 2025
.
SUVIKALP aims to establish a scientific, transparent and standardised framework for identifying suitable post-mining land-use opportunities. It addresses the challenges associated with fragmented assessments, independent evaluation of multiple parameters and limited integration of community priorities in conventional mine repurposing decisions.
Scientific and Data-Driven Assessment
SUVIKALP brings together geo-mining characteristics, environmental conditions, infrastructure availability, resource constraints, financial considerations and socio-economic factors within a unified digital platform. Users can create a comprehensive site profile by entering relevant mine-specific information, enabling systematic assessment of potential repurposing alternatives against the characteristics and constraints of individual mine sites.
The platform employs a
Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM)
methodology based on
TOPSIS (Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution)
to evaluate and rank potential repurposing options. This approach facilitates objective comparison of alternatives against multiple parameters, providing stakeholders with transparent, consistent and evidence-based recommendations.
The assessment process follows a structured sequence comprising factor selection, generation of potential options, integration of community priorities, suitability assessment and final ranking. This enables mine owners, project proponents and government agencies to make informed decisions based on site-specific conditions rather than relying exclusively on subjective assessments.
Integrating Community Priorities through RECLAIM
Sustainable mine repurposing must address the aspirations of communities residing in mining regions. Accordingly, SUVIKALP integrates
RECLAIM – Community Engagement and Development Framework
to incorporate local priorities into the project evaluation process.
The framework facilitates systematic consideration of community preferences alongside technical feasibility, environmental suitability and economic considerations. This helps ensure that proposed redevelopment initiatives are aligned with local development needs, employment generation, livelihood opportunities, infrastructure development and long-term community benefits.
By bringing community perspectives into the decision-making process, SUVIKALP promotes a participatory approach to post-mining development, strengthening the linkage between mine closure, regional development and inclusive growth.
From Project Identification to Implementation: PRISM
A distinguishing feature of SUVIKALP is its
PRISM (Post-Mining Repurposing Implementation Strategic Model)
, which extends the platform beyond the identification and ranking of potential projects.
PRISM provides a structured approach to exploring implementation pathways, including project vision, repurposing strategies, investment dynamics, strategic structuring and monitoring. It is supported by an integrated knowledge repository comprising project concept notes, national and international case studies, sample tender documents, details of implementation agencies and best-practice resources.
This integrated approach enables stakeholders to move from identifying suitable opportunities towards understanding the practical requirements for project development and execution. It also facilitates knowledge sharing and provides reference materials to support informed planning and implementation.
Way Forward: Building an Implementation-Oriented Framework
The next phase of SUVIKALP will focus on expanding its adoption and strengthening the transition from project recommendations to implementation. Key priorities include:
Wider Adoption:
Expand SUVIKALP across closed and abandoned coal and lignite mines.
Project Development:
Convert recommendations into site-specific feasibility studies, concept notes and DPRs.
Institutional Convergence:
Strengthen coordination among government, industry, experts and implementation agencies.
Investment Mobilisation:
Explore funding and partnerships for viable mine repurposing projects.
Knowledge and Capacity Building
: Share best practices and build stakeholder capacity.
Monitoring and Evaluation:
Track implementation and assess environmental, economic and community benefits. Towards a Sustainable Post-Mining Future
SUVIKALP represents an important step towards institutionalising scientific and participatory decision-making in mine repurposing. By integrating technical assessment, community priorities, objective project ranking and implementation guidance within a single digital ecosystem, it provides a structured foundation for sustainable post-mining land-use planning.
The long-term vision is to evolve SUVIKALP into a scalable national knowledge and decision-support ecosystem, adaptable to diverse mining conditions and regional development priorities. The success of this initiative will ultimately be reflected not merely in the identification of suitable projects, but in their successful implementation and the lasting benefits delivered to mining communities.
Through SUVIKALP, the objective is to transform the legacy of mining from resource extraction into an opportunity for environmental restoration, economic diversification and sustainable regional development.

title: APEDA Facilitates Export of 1.3 MT of Sinduri Pomegranates from Kullu to Dubai
subtitle: Export Initiative Links 600 Farmers Associated with Bhuntar FPO to International Markets
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 4:42PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India, facilitated the export of 1.3 metric tonnes (MT) of Sinduri variety pomegranates from Kullu district of Himachal Pradesh to Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE).
The consignment, comprising 650 boxes of 2 kg each, was exported by Uttar Pradesh-based Amama Exports. The initiative connects local growers and a Farmer Producer Organisation (FPO) with an exporter, creating opportunities for Himachal Pradesh’s horticultural produce to access international markets. The pomegranates were sourced directly from local farmers and the Bhuntar FPO, which is associated with approximately 600 farmers. The Kullu district horticulture administration supported the initiative by facilitating procurement and coordination.
The Sinduri variety is among the pomegranate varieties grown in Himachal Pradesh, alongside Bhagwa and Kandhari. Known for its attractive red skin, juicy arils and sweet-tart flavour, Sinduri pomegranates are suitable for fresh consumption and offer potential for export markets.
The initiative demonstrates the role of direct procurement and collective participation through FPOs in strengthening market linkages for farmers. The export enabled participating farmers to achieve 50% higher price realisation compared with the prevailing domestic market benchmark. Such export-oriented linkages can provide additional marketing opportunities for growers, encourage quality-focused production and support greater participation of FPOs in agricultural exports.
During FY 2025-26, India exported APEDA-scheduled agricultural and processed food products worth approximately USD 2.59 billion, with a total volume of around 3.81 million MT, to the UAE. The market offers opportunities for Himachal Pradesh’s horticultural produce, subject to buyer demand, quality requirements and applicable import regulations.
The consignment was officially flagged off by Chairman, APEDA, Shri Abhishek Dev. The ceremony was attended by APEDA officers, representatives of the Horticulture Department, exporters, FPOs and participating farmers. The programme highlighted the importance of coordination among farmers, producer organisations, exporters and government agencies in developing export opportunities for regional horticultural produce.
The export of Kullu pomegranates to Dubai adds to efforts to diversify Himachal Pradesh’s agricultural export basket beyond its established apple trade. The state has potential to explore overseas markets for other products, including pomegranates, persimmons, stone fruits, juices and ready-to-eat products. Continued focus on quality management, market linkages and export compliance can help expand opportunities for local growers and strengthen the state’s participation in international agricultural trade.
Through its export facilitation initiatives, APEDA continues to support Indian exporters, farmers and FPOs in accessing international markets and expanding the global reach of India’s agricultural and processed food products.

title: APEDA Facilitates Trial Export of 1.5 MT of Arunachal Pradesh Kiwi to Dubai
subtitle: “Kiwi: USP of Arunachal Pradesh” Initiative Aims to Strengthen Export Linkages for Local Growers
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 4:39PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India, facilitated the trial export of 1.5 metric tonnes (MT) of kiwi from Ziro, Arunachal Pradesh, to Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE). The consignment successfully reached Dubai and was showcased at LuLu Hypermarket, Al Qusais. The initiative marks a step towards assessing the fruit’s potential in international markets.
The initiative, undertaken under the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (MDoNER), seeks to promote and strengthen Arunachal Pradesh’s kiwi sector under the branding initiative “Kiwi: USP of Arunachal Pradesh”. Implemented in collaboration with the Department of Trade & Commerce and the Department of Horticulture, Government of Arunachal Pradesh, the initiative aims to introduce the state’s kiwis to international markets, assess consumer response and develop stronger market linkages to expand export opportunities for local growers.
Arunachal Pradesh’s high-altitude growing conditions and natural environment support the cultivation of kiwi with distinctive fruit quality and flavour. The state’s produce offers potential in premium domestic markets, export promotion and value-added products. The major varieties grown in the region include Hayward, Monty, Allison and Bruno, with the Hayward variety showing good demand in international markets.
With the consignment reaching retail shelves at LuLu Hypermarket, Al Qusais, the initiative has moved beyond the flag-off stage to retail-level market assessment. Consumer tasting and feedback will help evaluate the fruit’s acceptability and potential demand. The assessment is also expected to provide insights into consumer preferences, quality expectations, packaging and presentation requirements. These findings can help growers, cooperatives and exporters prepare for future commercial shipments and identify suitable market opportunities.
The initiative also seeks to connect local kiwi growers with potential overseas markets, creating additional sales channels and opportunities for improved farmer returns through future shipments. The trial export is expected to provide a basis for assessing market response and identifying requirements for expanding the presence of Arunachal Pradesh kiwi in international markets.
The flag-off ceremony was attended by the Minister of Agriculture & Allied Departments, Government of Arunachal Pradesh, Shri Gabriel D. Wangsu, and the MLA-cum-Advisor to the Minister of Trade & Commerce, Dr. Mohesh Chai. Other dignitaries present included the MLA, Ziro, Shri Hage Appa; Special Secretary (Agriculture/Horticulture), Ms. Rishita Gupta; Secretary, Trade & Commerce, Ms. Bullo Mamu, IRS; Secretary, Horticulture, Government of Arunachal Pradesh, Ms. Koj Rinya; and Director, ICER, Shillong, Shri Kardirvel Govindasamy.
Representatives of the Kiwi Growers Cooperative Society and Fair Exports India Pvt. Ltd. also participated in the event, along with APEDA officials, officers from the Departments of Trade & Commerce, Horticulture and Agriculture, kiwi farmers accompanying the consignment and other programme representatives.
Through this initiative, APEDA continues to support the promotion of agricultural and horticultural produce from the Northeast and facilitate its access to international markets. The successful arrival and retail placement of Arunachal Pradesh kiwi in Dubai provide an opportunity to evaluate overseas market potential and prepare local growers for participation in international trade.

title: Commerce and Industry Minister Shri Piyush Goyal Calls Upon Youth to Lead India’s Journey Towards Becoming a Developed Nation by 2047
subtitle:
India sets an ambitious target of $1 trillion in exports for the current year, registering 14 per cent growth so far: Shri Piyush Goyal

India has emerged as a trusted global partner, with countries across regions keen to enter into preferential trade agreements and free trade agreements with it: Shri Goyal
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 2:09PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal called upon young people to be ambitious, embrace transformation and contribute to nation-building while delivering the keynote address at the Young Leaders Discourse Forum at Kirori Mal College, New Delhi, today.
He underscored that achieving the goal of a developed India by 2047 was non-negotiable and that today's youth would be the architects of the country's journey towards this milestone. He observed that the students would be in their forties when India celebrates 100 years of independence, and that their choices, aspirations and contributions would define the country's future.
Highlighting India's export performance, Shri Goyal said that the country had recorded its highest-ever exports of USD 863 billion last year. He noted that while the International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its projections in April-May this year, had estimated global trade growth at 1.9 per cent, India had chosen to set an ambitious export target of USD 1 trillion for the current year, representing 16 per cent growth.
He said that India could have set an export target of USD 900 billion, representing 5 per cent growth over the previous year's exports, which would itself have been a significant achievement in view of the projected growth in global trade. A target of USD 900 billion would also have represented growth at more than twice the projected global trade growth rate. However, India chose to set a more ambitious target of USD 1 trillion. Shri Goyal expressed confidence that the country would achieve this milestone, noting that exports had already registered 14 per cent growth during the first six months of the financial year (April–September), reaching USD 480 billion. He said that India would need to achieve exports worth USD 520 billion in the remaining six months to meet the annual target and observed that October had also been a good month.
He further noted that the IMF had recently revised its projection for global trade growth to around 3.5 per cent, observing that India's export performance could have been one of the factors behind the revision.
Emphasising on India's growing stature in the global economy, Shri Goyal said that the country had come a long way from being a fragile five economy to becoming one of the world's leading economies and the fastest-growing large economy. Referring to a recent World Bank report, he noted that around 50 crore people in India had come out of extreme poverty and were making progress towards improving their lives through hard work.
He attributed India's growth to several factors, including its talent pool, the skills of its young population, its democratic system, a youthful demographic profile with an average age below 30 years, decisive leadership and the demand generated by 140 crore Indians for quality goods and services. He said that these strengths collectively provided impetus to India's growth story.
Shri Goyal said that India had earned the trust of the world, with countries across almost every region keen to enter into preferential trade agreements and free trade agreements with it. He observed that India was increasingly seen as a trusted partner, with its youthful population, talent, willingness to work hard and commitment to contributing to global growth strengthening its international standing.
Recalling India's support to countries during difficult times, he said that India had provided vaccines to the world during COVID-19 while ensuring free vaccination for every Indian. He also highlighted India's contribution through the provision of medicines and relief and rehabilitation assistance during crises, irrespective of whether the countries concerned were developed or less developed. He said that the recognition and respect India received across the world reflected the trust it had built through its actions.
Calling upon students to adopt an ambitious outlook, Shri Goyal asked them whether they would prefer to settle for modest targets or aspire for a better future. He said that transformation required a change in the way people think, work and live. He urged young people to continuously reinvent themselves, remain open to changing circumstances and pursue knowledge throughout their lives.
Emphasising the importance of educational institutions in shaping individuals, Shri Goyal said that colleges provide academic grooming while also building character, resilience, confidence and the willingness to work hard. They help shape how young people view their future and prepare them to play an important role in the destiny of the country. Drawing from his own experience, he said that students often do not fully appreciate the contribution of their school and college years while they are going through them. It is only when they enter the real world that they recognise how teachers, the academic environment and the overall grooming received during these formative years have shaped their lives and prepared them to become responsible citizens. Ultimately, he said, success lies in one's own hands.
He also acknowledged the contribution of teachers in shaping the lives and futures of students, noting that the impact of their guidance and the educational environment becomes more apparent as individuals progress in life.
Sharing his own academic journey, Shri Goyal spoke about the flexibility introduced through the National Education Policy, which allows students to change courses, earn credits for their academic work and move from one stream to another. He said that today's students were fortunate to have opportunities to pursue their dreams in an environment that offered greater flexibility.
Shri Goyal said that today's students were fortunate because they had a wider range of opportunities and could pursue careers of their choice. With almost the entire country becoming digitalised and 1.1 billion internet users, young people were connected to the world and had access to a substantial part of their knowledge and experiences online. He described this as a significant opportunity for students to learn, develop and contribute to India's growth.
Concluding his address, Shri Goyal emphasised the importance of keeping traditions alive and maintaining discipline within institutions. He said that discipline and respect for tradition formed the foundation of an organisation. He encouraged students to lead their lives with discipline, keep a larger goal in mind and never lose self-confidence or courage, emphasising that those who demonstrate courage ultimately succeed.

title: TRAI releases “The Telecommunication Interconnection (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2026”
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 12:37PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) today released
“The Telecommunication Interconnection (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2026”
. These regulations will take effect from 1st January, 2027.
Interconnection in telecommunications refers to the technical, operational, and commercial arrangements that connect two or more telecom networks, allowing telecommunications traffic to flow between them and enabling users of different service providers to communicate seamlessly. Section 11(1)(b) of the TRAI Act, 1997,
inter alia
, empowers TRAI to prescribe the terms and conditions of interconnection between service providers, and ensure technical compatibility and effective interconnection between different service providers.
To ensure that the existing regulatory framework governing interconnection matters remains relevant, transparent, and conducive to efficient interconnection between service providers, TRAI initiated the review of the regulatory framework through a Pre-Consultation Paper on the “Review of the existing TRAI Regulations on Interconnection matters”, dated 03.04.2025. Through this Pre-Consultation Paper, stakeholders’ comments were sought,
inter alia
, to review the Telecommunication Interconnection Regulations, 2018.
Subsequently, a Consultation Paper on the “Review of the existing TRAI Regulations on Interconnection matters”, providing the background information and taking into account the stakeholders’ comments received during the pre-consultation process, was issued on 10.11.2025. Through the Consultation Paper, stakeholders’ comments were sought,
inter alia
, to review the Telecommunication Interconnection Regulations, 2018. After extension, the last dates for furnishing written comments and counter-comments were 15.12.2025 and 29.12.2025, respectively.
In response to the issues raised in the Consultation Paper, seventeen stakeholders submitted their comments, while nine stakeholders submitted counter-comments. As part of the consultation process, an Open House Discussion (OHD) on the Consultation Paper was held on 28.01.2026. Based on the comments received from stakeholders during the consultation process, and their analysis, TRAI has finalised the Telecommunication Interconnection (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2026.
The salient points of the amendment regulations are given below:
Interconnection at LSA/ Service Area level
: The amendment enables interconnection providers and seekers to mutually agree on locations for handing over or taking over telecommunication traffic. It modernises the existing interconnection regulatory framework to align with contemporary network architectures and facilitate a transition from the existing interconnection at Long Distance Charging Area (LDCA) and Short Distance Charging Area (SDCA) level to the Licensed Service Area (LSA) level of interconnection. The shifting of traffic to LSA-level POIs would simplify routing and support more efficient management of scarce numbering resources, and would also result in benefits such as lower latency, and enhanced service reliability.
Migration of existing traffic at the SDCA/ LDCA-level POIs
: Existing traffic, in terms of Minutes of Usage (MoUs), at the LDCA/SDCA-level points of interconnection (POIs) shall be migrated to LSA-level POIs within three years, in a phased manner. Thereafter, all traffic shall be handed over or taken over at the LSA or Service Area level POIs.
Migration to IP-based interconnection
: The amendment regulations provide for establishment of IP-based interconnection by service providers. All new interconnections established after these regulations come into force shall be IP-based interconnections. All existing POIs working on E1/ TDM-based interconnection shall be migrated to IP-based interconnection within a period of three years, in a phased manner. The migration to IP-based interconnection improves bandwidth efficiency, call quality and end-to-end call performance.
Capacity augmentation framework for IP-based interconnection
: For IP-based interconnection, maximum call-handling capacity at a POI shall be determined having regard to the concurrent session-handling capability and link bandwidth, while maintaining the desired Quality of Service in accordance with the TRAI’s relevant Regulations.
Procedure for surrender of POIs
: A specific regulatory framework has been introduced for surrender of POIs. Earlier, the regulations had only the provision of “disconnection” of a POI, which is for stoppage of exchange of traffic at the POI. This is a step taken by a service provider for reasons attributable to the other service provider, in exceptional circumstances arising out of differences between them. On the other hand, the process for surrender is intended for voluntary surrender of a POI by a service provider for its own operational requirements, such as on account of reduction in traffic, withdrawal of services from an area or re-routing of traffic, thereby improving financial efficiency.
Rationalisation of bank guarantee provisions
: The existing bank guarantee framework has been retained; however, the validity of bank guarantees furnished on reassessment, and the interval for such reassessment, have been extended from six months to twelve months. A revised methodology has also been introduced for determining the ceiling on bank guarantees for POIs, including IP-based interconnection.
Interest on delayed payment of interconnection-related charges
: A specific provision has been introduced to address delayed payment of interconnection charges or interconnection usage charges. The rate of interest shall be mutually agreed between service providers, subject to a ceiling of the State Bank of India’s one-year Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate (MCLR) plus two percent.
Reporting requirements
: The amendment regulations prescribe reporting requirements for monitoring the shifting of traffic from LDCA/SDCA-level POIs to LSA-level POIs, and migration from E1/TDM-based to IP-based interconnection.
Graded framework for financial disincentives
: For effective implementation of the regulations, a graded financial disincentive framework has been prescribed for contravention of provisions of these regulations. This revision makes the enforcement of regulatory framework more effective, proportionate and commensurate with the nature and seriousness of the contraventions covered under these Regulations.
The provisions for interest on delayed payment, reporting requirements and financial disincentives will enable effective enforcement of the regulations. The amendment regulations align the regulatory provisions with technological advancements and sectoral developments. They are expected to strengthen the interconnection framework and facilitate seamless communication across telecom networks. The regulatory framework aims to provide greater regulatory certainty to service providers while upholding the principles of effective interconnection, transparency, non-discrimination and fair competition.
The full text of “The Telecommunication Interconnection (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2026”, along with the Explanatory Memorandum, is available on TRAI’s website
www.trai.gov.in
.

adv-nsl1@trai.gov.in
or telephone number +91-11-20907752.

title: Devotees Offer Prayers and Pay Homage to Sacred Relics of Lord Buddha at Tawang Monastery
subtitle:
Large Numbers of Devotees Gather at Tawang Monastery to Seek Blessings of Holi relics

Special Exhibitions at the Monastery Showcase the Archaeological, Historical and Cultural Legacy of Buddhism
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 5:28PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Sacred Exposition of the Holy Relics of Shakyamuni Buddha at Gaden Namgyal Lhatse (Tawang Monastery) has become a significant occasion of spiritual devotion and reverence for devotees from  Tawang and neighbouring regions of Arunachal Pradesh. During the first three days of the exposition, the monastery witnessed a large gathering of devotees, with long queues of people waiting to have a glimpse of the sacred relics, offer prayers and pay homage. The participation reflects the deep faith and devotion of the people towards Lord Buddha and his timeless teachings.
The exposition has been made accessible to Buddhist monks, senior citizens and the general public, providing devotees with an opportunity to pay homage to the sacred relics and experience their spiritual significance. It has also offered a rare opportunity for people to reconnect with the Buddha's enduring message of compassion, peace, wisdom and universal brotherhood.
Alongside the sacred exposition, visitors are being provided an opportunity to explore the rich heritage and diverse dimensions of Buddhist civilization through two special exhibitions. The exhibition titled ‘Unearthing the Sacred Piprahwa: The Story of the Holy Buddha Relics and Their Discovery’ Conducted by The International Buddhist Confederation (IBC), traces the archaeological history of the Piprahwa relics, highlighting their discovery in 1898 and their significance in Buddhist history. Another exhibition, ‘Crossroads of Dhamma: Classical Legacies, Living Art, and Anthropological Perspectives’, curated by the National Museum, New Delhi, showcases the historical, artistic and cultural evolution of Buddhism. Together, these exhibitions provide visitors with deeper insights into the rich and enduring legacy of Buddhism.
The sacred relics of Shakyamuni Buddha, brought from the National Museum, New Delhi, were ceremonially received by the Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh, Shri Pema Khandu, at the historic Tawang Monastery. The occasion was attended by Union Minister of Culture and Tourism, Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, along with venerable Buddhist monks, religious leaders and devotees, marking the commencement of the exposition in the state.
The exposition will continue at Tawang Monastery until November 7, 2026. Thereafter, the sacred relics will be taken to TGL Monastery (Lower Gompa), Bomdila, where they will be open for public veneration from November 8 to 13, 2026. The exposition will subsequently move to the Golden Pagoda, Namsai, from November 14 to 20, 2026. The sacred relics are scheduled to return to the National Museum, New Delhi, on November 21, 2026.

title: IPRD-2026 COMMENCES AT NEW DELHI, TRANSLATING SCIENTIFIC ADVANCEMENT INTO REGIONAL COOPERATION
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 6:18PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Indo-Pacific Regional Dialogue 2026 (IPRD-2026), the Indian Navy’s annual apex-level
international strategic dialogue
, commenced on
03 Nov 2026
at New Delhi. Organised in association with the National Maritime Foundation (NMF), the Navy’s knowledge partner, the
three-day
conference is examining
‘Science, Technology and Academic Cooperation in the Indo-Pacific’
, with particular emphasis on translating scientific advancement and institutional partnerships into practical regional cooperation.
The opening day of IPRD-2026 established the central question of the dialogue: ‘How the Indo-Pacific can turn scientific knowledge and technological innovation into enduring institutional cooperation, stronger maritime capabilities and shared regional resilience.’
The proceedings began with the Inaugural Address by Adm Dinesh K Tripathi (Retd), Chairman NMF, and former Chief of the Naval Staff. This was followed by a Special Address by VAdm Biswajit Dasgupta (Retd), National Maritime Security Coordinator, Govt of India.
The first session of IPRD-2026 focused upon the theme,
‘Academic Networks, Research, and Human Capital Development’
.  This session was moderated by VAdm Sanjay Mahindru (Retd), former Deputy Chief of the Naval Staff, and featured perspectives from
France, Indonesia, Japan and Maldives.
It explored the potential for a wider Indian Ocean academic network, including cooperation among universities in Indo-Pacific coastal cities, and examined social-science research networks in the Indian Ocean. The session also explored closer links among think tanks, universities and governments. A monograph entitled, ‘Sea Blindness and Maritime Heritage in India’, was also released upon culmination of this session.
The second professional session of the day,
‘Maritime Situational Awareness and Protection of Critical Maritime Infrastructure’,
highlighted the breadth of the contemporary maritime-awareness challenges associated with the protection of seaborne trade and critical undersea infrastructure. Moderated by VAdm Tarun Sobti (Retd), former Deputy Chief of the Naval Staff, it examined the opportunities and challenges associated with the Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness (IPMDA), particularly the practical requirements of information-sharing, and explored the development of cooperative Indo-Pacific architecture for underwater domain awareness. The session also included views from the Indian Ocean Commission (IOC) on cooperative approaches to the protection of critical maritime infrastructure.
Together, the two professional sessions examined how technological systems and scientific partnerships can be made operationally useful by strengthening maritime information-sharing, safeguarding critical infrastructure, improving access to oceanographic knowledge, and enabling a more coordinated response to climate-related risks.
The day’s programme also featured
‘Sahyog Ka Samvaad’
,
a special ambassadorial interaction
with HE Ms Mahishini Colonne, High Commissioner of Sri Lanka; HE Mr Josel F Ignacio, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Embassy of the Philippines; and HE Mrs May-Elin Stener, Ambassador of the Kingdom of Norway. This interaction was hosted and moderated by VAdm Pradeep Chauhan (Retd), Director-General, NMF.
The first day of IPRD-2026 ended on a highly optimistic note, with enthusiastic participation from the audience, that presented several actionable policy recommendations on fostering regional cooperation in science and technology, and knowledge sharing through academic collaboration.

title: Indigenous production & independent sustenance of critical defence capabilities key for military preparedness in 21st century: Raksha Mantri at Delhi Defence Dialogue 2026
subtitle:
“Defence reforms, Aatmanirbharta, collaborations & exports are interconnected pillars of Viksit Bharat@2047”

Shri Rajnath Singh calls for balancing operational requirements with research freedom to drive innovation

“Self-reliance is not a retreat from the world; it positions India better for global collaborations”

RM advocates international partnerships based on co-development, co-production & shared innovation
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                03 NOV 2026 5:44PM by PIB Delhi
content:
“Military preparedness in the 21st century is intrinsically linked to technological and industrial capabilities,” said Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh as he called for indigenous production of critical equipment and technologies and building the capacity to sustain them independently. Addressing the third edition of the Delhi Defence Dialogue at Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (MP-IDSA) on November 3, 2026, he emphasised that ‘Aatmanirbharta’ must be viewed as a quest for technological sovereignty as self-reliance means ensuring that the nation's critical defence requirements are not held hostage to external dependencies. True self-reliance is achieved by possessing the knowledge to design a defence platform, the technology to manufacture it, intellectual property to improve it and the capability to sustain it throughout its lifecycle, he said.
Sharing his insights on the theme of this year's Dialogue,
‘Defence Reforms, Aatmanirbharta, Collaborations and Exports’
, Raksha Mantri described the four elements as interconnected dimensions of India's objective to become Viksit Bharat by 2047. He stated that reforms must create an enabling institutional environment, Aatmanirbharta must strengthen indigenous technological capabilities, collaborations must accelerate access to advanced technologies and facilitate co-development, and exports must provide the scale, competitiveness and global partnerships required for a sustainable industrial ecosystem. These four elements are mutually reinforcing pillars of India's quest for strategic autonomy, he said.
Shri Rajnath Singh underlined that reforms represent the nation's willingness to change, Aatmanirbharta symbolises its determination to create, collaborations reflect its confidence to partner with the world, and exports demonstrate its readiness to compete globally. He emphasised that these four elements must progress together, as self-reliance without reforms, international collaborations and exports would limit India's technological horizons, industrial scale and global competitiveness.
Raksha Mantri pointed out that recent conflicts across the world have demonstrated a fundamental transformation in the character of warfare, with battlefields extending beyond land, sea and air into space, cyberspace and the digital domain. He stated that the distinction between conventional and unconventional warfare is increasingly blurring, while relatively inexpensive drones and autonomous systems are challenging sophisticated and costly military platforms. The ability to innovate rapidly, manufacture at scale and replenish capabilities has become as important as possessing advanced weapon systems, he added.
Highlighting that technological and manufacturing capabilities require an enabling institutional environment, progressive policies and responsive processes, Shri Rajnath Singh outlined the initiatives undertaken over the last decade to strengthen India's domestic defence industrial base. These include the establishment of Defence Industrial Corridors and the corporatisation of the erstwhile Ordnance Factory Board into seven Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs), aimed at enhancing autonomy, efficiency and competitiveness in defence manufacturing.
Raksha Mantri reiterated the Government's commitment to encouraging greater private sector participation in the development and manufacturing of advanced defence platforms and systems. “Opportunities for private participation in programmes such as the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft, propulsion systems, ATAGS, artillery ammunition and shipbuilding will accelerate indigenous development, expand manufacturing capacity and strengthen India's position in the global defence market. These initiatives are creating opportunities for wider participation by private industry, MSMEs, start-ups and academia,” he said.
Shri Rajnath Singh highlighted that 2025 was observed as the Year of Reforms in the Ministry of Defence, with a focus on jointness, integration, emerging technologies, innovation and strengthening the domestic defence industrial ecosystem. He said that reforms initiated across policies, institutional structures, technology development, acquisition procedures and ease of doing business are yielding positive results, with defence production reaching a record level of approximately Rs 1.78 lakh crore in FY 2025-26 and defence exports rising to Rs 38,424 crore. Indian defence products are now reaching more than 80 countries, reflecting the growing contribution of public sector enterprises, private industry, MSMEs and start-ups, he added.
Raksha Mantri described defence exports as a crucial dimension of India's self-reliance agenda, stating that exports reflect the maturity of the domestic industrial ecosystem, the competitiveness of indigenous technologies and the confidence of international partners in India's capabilities. He attributed the growth to sustained policy liberalisation, simplification and standardisation, which have enabled Indian manufacturers, particularly MSMEs, to respond more effectively to international opportunities.
Shri Rajnath Singh called for expanding the scope of defence exports to include maintenance, repair, training, logistics and technology cooperation, stating that every successful export should become the foundation of an enduring strategic partnership. He reiterated the Government's resolve to achieve the targets of Rs 3 lakh crore in defence production and Rs 50,000 crore in defence exports by 2029. The domestic defence industry must expand manufacturing capacity, improve quality and strengthen global competitiveness to achieve these objectives, he said.
Raksha Mantri emphasised that the Defence Forces must remain important stakeholders in the R&D process, as their operational experience and understanding of the battlefield are invaluable in informing research priorities and assessing the relevance of emerging technologies. At the same time, he stressed the need to look beyond the immediate requirements of the end-user in the research process. He observed that research driven too closely by immediate operational perceptions could end up addressing only recognised problems, rather than exploring possibilities that may not yet have been imagined. R&D must have the freedom to question established assumptions, pursue unconventional ideas and discover technologies whose applications may not be immediately apparent, he said.
Shri Rajnath Singh called for striking the right balance by allowing operational requirements to inform research while preserving the independence and intellectual space necessary for innovation. He underscored the importance of encouraging experimentation and ensuring that successful innovations move beyond laboratories and prototypes towards production and operational induction. The objective must be to create an ecosystem in which innovation is encouraged, investment is sustained and successful ideas are translated into capabilities, he said.
On international defence collaborations, Raksha Mantri asserted that India's pursuit of self-reliance does not signify a retreat from the world; it symbolises a confident and technologically capable India better positioned to engage with international partners. He noted that while traditional partnerships based on procurement, licensed manufacturing and transfer of technology have contributed to India's industrial capabilities, future requirements call for a more ambitious approach based on co-development, co-production and shared innovation.
“Such partnerships should ensure meaningful Indian participation in design and development, access to critical technologies, appropriate sharing of intellectual property and opportunities for Indian companies to participate in global supply chains. Our large domestic market, expanding industrial base and strong pool of scientific and engineering talent offer significant opportunities for international companies to partner with Indian industry,” said Shri Rajnath Singh.
Concluding his address, Raksha Mantri called for a collective commitment from the Defence Forces, civil servants, scientists, industry, academia and international partners to realise India's defence ambitions. He stated that the country's aspiration must be to move beyond procuring defence technologies towards creating them, beyond manufacturing for domestic requirements towards competing in global markets, and beyond participating in international defence partnerships towards contributing meaningfully to shaping the future of global defence technology. He expressed confidence that the deliberations at the Delhi Defence Dialogue would generate valuable ideas and actionable recommendations towards achieving this vision.
In his welcome remarks, Director General, MP-IDSA, Ambassador Sujan R Chinoy highlighted that the Delhi Defence Dialogue 2026 would provide a platform for exchanging perspectives on defence reforms, indigenous capabilities, international collaborations and defence exports. He also referred to the two preparatory roundtables organised by MP-IDSA on propulsion systems and defence exports, as well as the inaugural ASEAN-India Defence Think Tank Forum, which further strengthened the Institute's international engagement.
CISC Air Marshal Tejinder Singh, Additional Secretary Smt Dipti Mohil Chawla, other senior serving & retired officials, and foreign dignitaries were present on the occasion.
About Delhi Defence Dialogue
The two-day dialogue, organised by MP-IDSA on November 3 & 4, 2026, brings together policymakers, representatives of the Defence Forces, defence industry, academia, think tanks and strategic experts from India and abroad to deliberate on India's evolving defence priorities and opportunities for international cooperation.
The deliberations are focused on generating actionable policy recommendations to strengthen India's defence preparedness, promote indigenous technological capabilities and expand opportunities for international defence cooperation. The dialogue seeks to facilitate greater engagement among the Government, industry, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), MSMEs, start-ups and research institutions. The outcomes are expected to provide valuable inputs for policy formulation and contribute to advancing India's strategic vision of a self-reliant and technologically advanced defence ecosystem.
